html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Use ConfigMaps and Secrets and say what protects a Secret
  • Set requests and limits, and apply LimitRange and ResourceQuota
  • Describe cluster setup, upgrades, version skew and etcd backup
  • Take a node out of service safely with cordon, drain and PodDisruptionBudgets

2ConfigMaps, using configuration, what the exam asks

Running case

Harbor Books Runs the Shop for Real

  • Settings such as the database host and the payment key must not live in the image
  • The shop must not starve other teams, and the platform engineer wants a quota for it
  • One worker node needs patching, and the cluster needs upgrades and backups
  • In this module you set up configuration, limits and routine maintenance

ConfigMaps

  • A ConfigMap stores non-confidential settings as key-value pairs, separate from the code
  • The same image can run in development and in production with different ConfigMaps
  • data holds text values; binaryData holds binary values
  • A ConfigMap is limited to 1 MiB, and it gives no secrecy or encryption

Settings for the shop

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: shop-config
data:
  DATABASE_HOST: postgres
  LOG_LEVEL: info
Exam tip

Anything you would be happy to see in a public repository belongs in a ConfigMap; anything confidential does not.

Using a ConfigMap in a Pod

  • As environment variables: envFrom loads every key, and configMapKeyRef picks one key
  • As files in a read-only volume mounted into the container
  • The ConfigMap and the Pod must share a namespace

One ConfigMap used both ways

containers:
- name: storefront
  envFrom:
  - configMapRef:
      name: shop-config
  volumeMounts:
  - name: config
    mountPath: /etc/shop
volumes:
- name: config
  configMap:
    name: shop-config
Exam tip

A ConfigMap reaches a container as environment variables or as files.

What the Exam Asks: Configuration and Administration

  • ConfigMap or Secret: settings anyone may see, or confidential data
  • base64 or encryption: base64 only encodes; encryption at rest protects Secrets in etcd
  • Request or limit: requests place the Pod; limits are enforced
  • LimitRange or ResourceQuota: per object, or the whole namespace
  • Cordon or drain: cordon stops new Pods; drain also evicts the running ones
  • Upgrade order: control plane first, one minor version at a time
Exam tip

When a question names a limit, ask who enforces it: the scheduler, the kubelet or the kernel.

3Secrets and how to protect them

Secrets: Encoded, Not Encrypted

  • A Secret holds confidential values such as passwords, tokens and keys, outside Pod specs and images
  • Values in a manifest are base64-encoded: that is encoding, not encryption
  • By default Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd, and anyone with API or etcd access can read them
  • Protect them with encryption at rest, RBAC (role-based access control) with least privilege, access limited to specific containers, or an external secret store

Exam tip

base64 is not encryption.

4Requests and limits, LimitRange, ResourceQuota

Resource Requests and Limits

  • A request is what the container needs: the scheduler uses it to place the Pod, and the kubelet reserves it
  • A limit is the most it may use: the kubelet enforces it
  • CPU is measured in CPU units: 1 is one physical core, and 500m is half a core
  • Memory is measured in bytes, with suffixes such as Mi

Requests and limits on a container

containers:
- name: storefront
  image: harborbooks/storefront:1.4
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 250m
      memory: 64Mi
    limits:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 128Mi
Exam tip

Requests are for scheduling; limits are for enforcement.

What Requests and Limits Do

  • A container may use more than its request if the node has room to spare
  • Over its CPU limit, a container is throttled
  • Over its memory limit, the kernel may kill it, when memory is under pressure
  • So CPU limits slow a container down; memory limits can stop it

Exam tip

CPU is throttled; memory is killed.

LimitRange and ResourceQuota

  • A LimitRange constrains the requests and limits of each Pod or container: a minimum, a maximum, a ratio, and defaults
  • A ResourceQuota limits the total resources used in the namespace and the number of objects of a kind
  • The cluster administrator sets up at least one ResourceQuota per namespace

Exam tip

LimitRange shapes each object; ResourceQuota caps the namespace.

5Kubeadm, upgrades and version skew, etcd backup, node maintenance, releases and deprecation

Cluster Setup with kubeadm Beyond the curriculum

  • kubeadm init initializes the first control-plane node
  • Install a Pod network add-on so that Pods can communicate
  • kubeadm join, with a token, adds the other nodes
  • With several clusters, keep one kubeconfig context for each and switch with kubectl config use-context

Exam tip

init for the control plane, join for the rest.

Upgrades and Version Skew Beyond the curriculum Moving

  • Upgrade in order: the control plane first, then the worker nodes
  • Go one minor version at a time; skipping minor versions is not supported
  • Drain a node before a minor-version kubelet upgrade
  • As of 30 October 2026: the kubelet can lag the API server by up to three minor versions; the controller manager and scheduler by one

Exam tip

Components may lag the API server but never lead it.

etcd Backup and Restore

  • etcd holds all cluster data, so back it up
  • A backup is a snapshot, taken with etcdctl snapshot save
  • A restore uses etcdutl snapshot restore
  • etcdctl is the client that talks to etcd over the network; etcdutl works directly on etcd data files

Back up and restore etcd

ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints $ENDPOINT snapshot save snapshot.db
etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status snapshot.db
etcdutl --data-dir <data-dir-location> snapshot restore snapshot.db
Exam tip

Save with etcdctl; restore with etcdutl.

Node Maintenance: Cordon, Drain and PodDisruptionBudgets

  • cordon marks a node unschedulable: no new Pods land on it
  • drain safely evicts the Pods, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets; --ignore-daemonsets skips DaemonSet Pods
  • uncordon makes the node schedulable again
  • A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many Pods of an app may be down at once during voluntary disruptions such as a drain

Patch a node without taking the app down

kubectl cordon worker-2
kubectl drain worker-2 --ignore-daemonsets
kubectl uncordon worker-2
Exam tip

Drain first, patch second, uncordon last.

Releases, Deprecation and Support Moving

Topic The rule
Release cycle about three Kubernetes releases a year
Patch support about one year, plus two months of maintenance: 14 months
GA APIs (generally available) may be deprecated but are not removed within a major version
Beta APIs deprecated within 9 months or 3 releases, and no longer served 9 months or 3 releases after that, whichever is longer
Alpha APIs may be removed in any release without a deprecation notice
  • As of 30 October 2026: v1.37 is the latest minor release
Exam tip

Stable APIs are not removed within a major version; alpha ones can vanish at any time.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Which statement about ConfigMaps is correct?

  • AThey are stored encrypted in etcd, which makes them suitable for passwords and keys
  • BThey hold non-confidential settings as key-value pairs, apart from the code
  • CThey can hold large amounts of data, because a size limit does not apply to them
  • DThey can be read by Pods that run in a different namespace
Show the answer

Answer: B. A ConfigMap keeps non-confidential settings separate from the code. It gives no encryption, so it is not meant for passwords, it is limited to 1 MiB, and a Pod can use only ConfigMaps from its own namespace.

S2Harbor Books runs the same storefront image in staging and in production, with a different database host in each. What is the best way to supply the host?

  • AKeep it in a ConfigMap for each environment and pass it to the Pod
  • BBuild one image per environment with the host baked into its files
  • CStore it in a Secret, since every setting has to be kept confidential
  • DEdit the files inside the running container after each restart
Show the answer

Answer: A. A ConfigMap keeps settings apart from the image, so one image can serve both environments, and the Pod receives the value as an environment variable or a file. Building separate images defeats that, a database host is not confidential, and edits inside a container are lost on restart.

S3A Secret's value in a manifest is base64-encoded. What does that mean?

  • AThe value is encrypted and cannot be read without the cluster's own secret key
  • BThe value is hashed, so nobody can recover the original text
  • CThe value is compressed, so it takes less space in etcd and in the API server
  • DThe value is only encoded, so anyone who can read the Secret can decode it
Show the answer

Answer: D. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, so anyone who can read the Secret can decode it. By default Secrets are also stored unencrypted in etcd, which is why encryption at rest and tight access rules are recommended.

S4A Pod requests 500m of CPU and 256Mi of memory. What does the scheduler do with these requests?

  • AIt caps the container at those amounts for as long as the Pod keeps running
  • BIt ignores them unless a limit is also set on the container
  • CIt uses them to choose a node that has enough unreserved capacity
  • DIt terminates the Pod whenever it uses more than those amounts of either resource
Show the answer

Answer: C. The scheduler uses requests to decide which node can fit the Pod, and the kubelet reserves that amount for the container. Capping and terminating are enforcement of limits, not requests.

S5One container goes over its CPU limit and another goes over its memory limit. What happens?

  • AThe CPU is throttled, while the memory over-use can get the container killed
  • BBoth containers are terminated at once, because every limit is enforced as a hard stop
  • CBoth containers are throttled until they fall below their limits again
  • DBoth limits are raised automatically to match what the containers use
Show the answer

Answer: A. CPU limits are enforced by throttling, and memory limits by out-of-memory kills when the kernel sees memory pressure. Limits are not raised automatically, and CPU over-use does not terminate a container.

S6The platform engineer wants to cap the total CPU and memory that all Pods in the shop namespace can use together. Which object does that?

  • AA LimitRange, which caps the namespace's total usage of each resource
  • BA ResourceQuota, which limits aggregate consumption per namespace
  • CA PodDisruptionBudget, which limits how many Pods a namespace may run
  • DA ConfigMap, which carries the quota settings into every Pod
Show the answer

Answer: B. A ResourceQuota limits the total resources used in a namespace. A LimitRange constrains the requests and limits of each object, a PodDisruptionBudget limits voluntary disruption, and a ConfigMap only holds settings.

S7Which statement about upgrading a kubeadm cluster is correct?

  • AUpgrade the worker nodes first, and afterwards upgrade the control plane nodes
  • BSkip minor versions to reach the newest release in a single step
  • CUpgrade the control plane first, one minor version at a time, then the workers
  • DUpgrade the nodes together at the very same moment, so that the versions match each other
Show the answer

Answer: C. The control plane is upgraded first, then the worker nodes, and minor versions cannot be skipped. Components such as the kubelet may lag the API server but must not be newer than it.

S8How do you take a backup of the data in etcd?

  • ABy copying the kubelet's configuration directory to a safe place
  • BBy running kubeadm upgrade plan on the control plane node
  • CBy running kubectl get all and saving its output to a file
  • DBy taking a snapshot with etcdctl snapshot save against etcd
Show the answer

Answer: D. etcd is backed up with a snapshot, taken with etcdctl snapshot save and restored with etcdutl snapshot restore. The kubelet configuration and kubectl output do not hold the cluster's data, and kubeadm upgrade plan only reports available upgrades.

S9Harbor Books must patch a worker node without taking the storefront down. Which sequence is right?

  • AStop the kubelet, patch the node, and wait for the Pods to move on their own
  • BDelete the node object and let the scheduler recreate its Pods elsewhere
  • CDrain the node so the Pods are evicted gracefully, patch it, then uncordon it
  • DCordon the node and patch it at once, because cordon also moves the Pods away
Show the answer

Answer: C. Drain cordons the node and evicts its Pods safely, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, so the app keeps its minimum availability. Uncordon makes the node usable again afterwards. Cordon alone leaves the Pods running on the node.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Configuration ConfigMaps for non-confidential settings, as environment variables or files; Secrets for confidential data, protected beyond base64
Resources requests place Pods, limits are enforced; LimitRange shapes objects, ResourceQuota caps a namespace
Cluster setup kubeadm init and join, then a Pod network add-on
Upgrades and backups control plane first, one minor version at a time; snapshot etcd
Maintenance cordon, drain with PodDisruptionBudgets, uncordon
